subject: civil
audience: FE Civil candidates and civil engineering students
title: The Two Cables That Each Carried 10 kN
featured_title: THE TWO CABLES THAT EACH CARRIED 10 KN

presentation.challenge: A 10 kN load was shared by two cables, but each cable still carried 10 kN of tension.

practice.primary_question: Why can each of two symmetric cables carry 10 kN of tension while supporting only a 10 kN vertical load?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Dividing the load by two and calling 5 kN the cable tension without accounting for the cable angle.

case_dna.target_misconception: Two identical cables supporting a 10 kN load must each have only 5 kN tension.
case_dna.why_plausible: The vertical load is shared equally, so 5 kN is indeed the vertical component in each cable.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: Each cable is 30° above horizontal. Its vertical component is T sin30°. Equilibrium requires 2T sin30°=10 kN, so T=10 kN.
case_dna.corrected_model: Share the required force components, not the tension magnitudes. Resolve each cable force along the equilibrium axes.

problem_statement: A 10 kN load hangs from two identical cables arranged symmetrically, each cable making 30° above the horizontal. A field note states each cable carries 5 kN because the load is shared equally. Determine the actual cable tension, identify the component error, and choose a geometry change that reduces the cable force.
fixed_constraints: Initial cable angle is 30° above horizontal

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The load was 10 kN. Each cable measured 10 kN.
gates.prompt: Why is 5 kN only a component, not the cable tension?

options.label: Use 2T sin30° = 10 kN because only the vertical components support the load
options.reason: The horizontal components cancel by symmetry while the vertical components balance the load.

options.label: Use T = 10/2 = 5 kN directly
options.reason: That assigns the required vertical component as the full inclined cable tension.

options.label: Use 2T cos30° = 10 kN for an angle measured from horizontal
options.reason: For an angle from horizontal, the vertical component is T sinθ.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the cable tension
gates.prompt: What tension (kN) is required in each cable?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Read the cable force
gates.result: Each cable carries 10 kN of tension.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the equilibrium
gates.success: T = 10 kN. Each cable contributes 5 kN vertically.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The free-body diagram separates tension from its vertical component

cards.text: Each cable contributes T sin30° vertically.
The two horizontal components are equal and opposite.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the support-force note
report: C2. The two cables are symmetric.
C3. Therefore each cable tension is 5 kN.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: Five kilonewtons is the vertical component required from each cable, not the total inclined force.

evidence_choices.label: 2T sin30°=10 gives T=10 kN
evidence_choices.reason: This directly applies vertical equilibrium to the inclined forces.

correction.template: Each inclined cable must carry {tension} kN so that its vertical component is 5 kN.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Reduce cable tension without changing the 10 kN load

options.label: Increase the cable angle to 60° above horizontal
Reduce the angle to 15° above horizontal
options.reason: A shallower angle requires greater tension for the same vertical component.

options.label: Keep 30° but call 5 kN the tension
options.reason: Renaming the component does not change equilibrium.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply symmetric cable equilibrium
gates.prompt: A 12 kN load is supported by two symmetric cables at 90° above horizontal. What is the tension in each cable?

options.label: 6 kN
options.reason: At 90°, each cable is vertical, so 2T=12.

options.label: 0 kN
options.reason: The cables must support the load.

gates.explanation: When the cables are vertical, their full tensions act in the vertical direction.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the force resolution
gates.confirmation: I confirm that equilibrium must be written using force components based on the stated cable angle.

items.label: What failed
items.value: Cable tension was confused with the cable's vertical component.

items.label: What was assumed
items.value: Equal load sharing meant each tension was half the load.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Resolve each inclined force and enforce ΣFx=0 and ΣFy=0.

seo.seo_title: Cable Tension Equilibrium: Why Two Cables Each Carry 10 kN | FE E-041
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Civil Case E-041: two 30° cables support a 10 kN load, yet each cable carries 10 kN. Resolve force components and verify equilibrium.
seo.excerpt: Equal load sharing does not mean the inclined cable tension equals half the vertical load.
seo.direct_answer: For two symmetric cables at 30° above horizontal supporting 10 kN, vertical equilibrium gives 2T sin30°=10. Since sin30°=0.5, each cable tension is 10 kN even though each cable contributes only 5 kN vertically.

faqs.q: Why is cable tension larger than half the supported load?
faqs.a: Only the vertical component of an inclined cable tension supports the load.

faqs.q: How does a steeper cable angle affect tension?
faqs.a: For the same vertical load, a steeper angle above horizontal increases the vertical component per unit tension and reduces required tension.
